readingInstruction: Read Acts 17:1-18:28. Paul preaches in Thessalonica, is received nobly in Berea, speaks to the philosophers at Athens, and stays a year and a half in Corinth. Read the Areopagus speech (17:22-31) slowly.
settingTheScene: Paul and Silas travel southwest from Philippi through Amphipolis and Apollonia to Thessalonica. Opposition drives them to Berea, then Paul goes on to Athens, the intellectual capital of the Greek world. Finally, he reaches Corinth, a wealthy and immoral port city, where he stays eighteen months. Along the way he meets Priscilla and Aquila.
observation: “Explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead” (17:2-3).
“Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so” (17:11).

“For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: To the unknown god. What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you” (17:23).
“The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man” (17:24).
“In him we live and move and have our being” (17:28).
“Because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (17:31).
“Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you” (18:9-10).
“They took him and explained to him the way of God more accurately” (18:26).
interpretation:
In Thessalonica, Paul reasons from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths, explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that Jesus is the Christ. Some believe, including many God-fearing Greeks, but jealous Jews form a mob. The accusation is that they are “turning the world upside down” and saying there is another king, Jesus. In Berea, the Jews are more noble: they receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily to see if these things are so. This is the model for every Christian: test what you hear against the Bible.

At Athens, Paul is provoked by a city full of idols. He argues in the synagogue and the marketplace, and the philosophers bring him to the Areopagus. His speech is a model of cross-cultural preaching. He begins with their religiosity and the altar to an unknown god. Then he proclaims the God who made the world and everything in it, who does not live in temples made by man or need anything from human hands, and who gives to all mankind life and breath. He made from one man every nation, having determined their allotted periods and boundaries, that they should seek God. He quotes their own poets: “In him we live and move and have our being” and “We are his offspring.” Since we are God’s offspring, we ought not to think the divine being is like gold or silver or stone. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day to judge the world in righteousness by a man he has appointed, and has given assurance by raising him from the dead. Some mock at the resurrection, some want to hear more, and a few believe, including Dionysius and a woman named Damaris.

In Corinth, Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, fellow tentmakers, and works with them. He preaches in the synagogue, and when the Jews oppose, he turns to the Gentiles. Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believes. The Lord appears to Paul in a night vision: “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.” He stays a year and a half. At the end of the chapter, Apollos, an eloquent man mighty in the Scriptures, comes to Ephesus, and Priscilla and Aquila, hearing him, take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately. A husband and wife team the gifted teacher.
connection: Isaiah 44:9-20 mocks idols. Psalm 115:3-8 also. Deuteronomy 32:8 speaks of God setting the boundaries of nations. Isaiah 42:5 says God gives breath to the people. Romans 1:18-25 discusses the suppression of the truth. Romans 2:14-16 describes the law written on hearts. 1 Corinthians 2:1-5 shows Paul’s approach at Corinth. 1 Corinthians 16:19 mentions Aquila and Priscilla. 2 Timothy 3:16-17 says all Scripture is God-breathed. Acts 24:15 speaks of the resurrection of the just and unjust.
application:
Be a Berean: check what you hear, including from me, against Scripture.

Learn to listen to the culture and find a bridge, like the altar, to speak of Christ.

Be like Priscilla and Aquila: take aside a gifted person who needs help and teach them.
prayerPrompts: Praise God as the one in whom we live and move and have our being.
Ask him for the nobility of Berea, to examine Scripture daily.
Pray for the people you know who worship the unknown.
